question.text: Subclavian steal syndrome: can the blood pressure difference between arms predict the severity of steal?
question.context: A side-to-side difference in systolic brachial arterial blood pressure is a common finding in subclavian artery stenosis and is frequently used as a screening tool for subclavian steal syndrome (SSS). It was the goal of this retrospective study to investigate the relationship between different vertebral artery waveform types and the side-to-side difference in systolic blood pressure in patients with sonographically proven SSS. The records of 1860 patients from the Neuroultrasound Laboratory between January 2000 and December 2000 were screened for the diagnosis of SSS in the final ultrasound report. In all patients, bilateral brachial arterial blood pressure was measured in a sitting position prior to the ultrasound examination. Vertebral artery waveforms were classified as (1) systolic deceleration, (2) alternating flow, and (3) complete reversal at rest. Blood pressure difference as calculated by normal-side blood pressure minus lesion-side blood pressure was compared with the 3 Doppler waveform types. SSS was found in 51 of 1860 (2.7%) ultrasonography studies of 49 patients (17 men, 32 women; mean age 65.3 +/- 10.5 years). Two patients (4%) had bilateral SSS. In 3 patients (6%), SSS was related to an innominate artery stenosis. Waveform analysis showed a completely reversed flow in 16 (31%), an alternating flow in 24 (47%), and a systolic deceleration in 11 (22%) cases. Systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating groups than in the systolic deceleration group (P<.001).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a significant correlation between the severity of the subclavian steal syndrome (complete reversal and alternating flow) and the blood pressure difference between the arms. This suggests that a greater blood pressure difference is associated with a more severe steal syndrome.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating groups than in the systolic deceleration group (P<.001).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could influence blood pressure, the study specifically investigated the relationship between vertebral artery waveform types and blood pressure difference, making the direct correlation more likely to be relevant to the severity of the steal syndrome.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates a statistically significant correlation (P<.001) between vertebral artery waveform types and systolic blood pressure difference, with higher pressure differences in complete reversal and alternating flow patterns compared to systolic deceleration. This supports the predictive value of blood pressure measurements in assessing SSS severity.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The significant association (P<.001) between waveform types and blood pressure difference demonstrates that pressure measurements can predict SSS severity
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While other vascular conditions could cause pressure differences, the specific waveform patterns observed in SSS provide a reliable diagnostic marker that supports the predictive relationship

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study directly demonstrates that systolic blood pressure difference correlates with vertebral artery waveform types, with significantly higher differences in complete reversal and alternating flow groups compared to systolic deceleration. This suggests that arm blood pressure difference can reflect the severity of steal physiology.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating groups than in the systolic deceleration group (P<.001).
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other causes of arm BP difference (e.g., atherosclerosis, hypertension) were not specifically evaluated, but the study focused on SSS patients with confirmed vertebral flow patterns, making waveform type the key differentiator.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other possible differentials include carotid artery stenosis, arterial occlusion, or collateral flow issues, but the case specifically focuses on SSS and its ultrasound/Doppler features. The absence of detailed clinical outcomes (e.g., neurological deficits, flow velocity, or perfusion status) means the BP difference alone is not proven to reliably predict SSS severity.
